Electron Beam Welding System Layout While the vacuum chamber and vacuum pumps can require a significant amount of floor space, the additional control cabinets, run-out tables and high voltage power cabinets require often unanticipated floor space requirements as shown in Figure 33. The chamber on the left is shown as an example of the large floor space required for all auxiliary systems, while the chamber on the right represents the scale of chamber required for electron beam welding of copper accelerators. Any loading/unloading systems or cranes, as well as shipping/receiving, assembly, and quality control stations will also need to be considered in the layout of a workspace that can accommodate EBW of high-gradient structure. Additional considerations regarding the facility housing the EBW facility are needed, with considerations such as a reliable power mains, humidity and temperature control, closed-loop water chillers for the pumps/gun, particulate control and floor loading capacity. Because of the high vacuum and high voltage sub-systems, electron beam welding systems are generally more complex to install and maintain than machining equipment, and also do not have such readily available replacement parts and/or service programs. The workflow is separated into Pre-Weld, Weld, and Post-Weld phases because standard welding economic calculations consider weld time as the critical determinant of value generation. The ratio of weld time to non-weld time is of critical importance to how many components can be manufactured per given period. Straight forward fabrication tasks on highly weldable alloys with simple geometries can be streamlined to minimize non-weld time. Jobs on exotic or low weldability alloys with complex geometries or assemblies require significantly more pre-weld time and iterative problem solving to complete which expands non-weld time and reduces profitability.
